title: Chess With a Thinking Break
summary: Help first-time chess club visitors use a beginner session and choose when to move toward a timed match.

documents.title: Beginners' table card
documents.text: Welcome to the first Saturday of our chess club. If you know little about the game, go to Table Three near the window. You do not have to finish a game there. First, one player reads a small card that says which pieces to put on the board. The other player puts the pieces in place. Change jobs for the next card. Each position gives you only a few pieces, so you can concentrate on the problem. Ask for a thinking break at any point. Both players stop moving pieces during the break. When you are ready to carry on, tell your partner before you touch a piece. We do not use a timer at Table Three. At Table Four, both players have ten minutes each. A helper can show you how to use the timer when your first game starts. If Table Three is full, do not join a timed game just because a seat is free. Put your name on the board by the window, and a helper will tell you when a place opens.

documents.title: Lucy explains the practice card
documents.text: Our first card asks the player with the dark pieces to make one move and then explain what the other player could do. You do not have to know the name of the move. You can point to the piece and say which square it will go to. If you want help, take one small blue card from the desk. The blue card does not give you the answer. It asks you to look again at one part of the board. There is a separate answer sheet in the drawer, but check it after you and your partner have each suggested a move. Last week we found that some people copied the answer and could not remember the reason later. One more tip: if someone moves a piece to explain a possible answer, return it to its first square before the other player has a go. Otherwise you are working on a new problem with the old instructions.

recordings.title: A first round with a new partner
recordings.text:
Ben: I think this is my first turn. I read the card while you place the pieces, is that right?

Rina: Yes. Can you say the second square again? I heard D, but I didn't hear the number.

Ben: D five. That's where the white piece goes. The dark piece starts one row below.

Rina: Like this? Good. Now I should suggest the first move. I'm going to take a thinking break, if that's okay.

Ben: Of course. I won't touch the board. Do you want the blue card?

Rina: Maybe in a minute. First, I'm checking what your white piece can do if I move the dark one. Okay, I'm ready now. I want to move this one here.

Ben: And I could move across like this. Wait, I'll put mine back so you can tell me your other idea.

Rina: Thanks. I can explain it without moving the piece this time. Can you point to the square I mean when I say it?

recordings.title: Choosing the next table
recordings.text:
Helper: I saw you finish two cards. Do you want a third, or would you like to try the timer at Table Four?

Ben: I'd like to see how the timer works. I don't know if I want to play a whole game with it yet.

Helper: You can watch this pair finish first. Notice how they press the button only after they finish moving the piece.

Ben: Could I try pressing it with a practice card? Rina doesn't want a timed match today.

Helper: Yes. At two, there is a short demonstration before the next game. You can have a go then. You should keep taking cards at Table Three until it is announced. Oh, there's another name waiting to sit with Rina if you decide to move tables.

Ben: I'll stay with her for this round, then speak to the helper by the window. I don't want to leave the dark pieces in the wrong places for the next pair.

reading.prompt: 1. At the beginners' table, when do partners exchange jobs?
options: After a player touches a piece
Before anyone can take a break
When Table Four has a free chair
When they start a new card
reading.explanation: The instructions ask players to switch the set-up and reading roles with each card.

reading.prompt: 1. What does the other player do during a thinking break?
options: Begins to play with a third person
reading.explanation: Both players leave the board unchanged during a break.

reading.prompt: 1. What should a beginner do when Table Three has no space?
options: Start a game at Table Four immediately.
Put a name on the board by the window.
Take home an answer sheet and return later.
Move a timed game to the window.
reading.explanation: The notice says to join the waiting list rather than take an unrelated free seat.

reading.prompt: 2. What kind of help does a blue card give?
options: It directs attention to part of the board.
It tells both players the correct move.
It gives the exact name of the move.
It changes which player moves first.
reading.explanation: The clue guides a second look, while answers are in a different place.

reading.prompt: 2. When should players use the full answer sheet?
options: Whenever the white player moves first
After both have offered a move
As soon as either one takes a blue card
Only once the room gets too full
reading.explanation: The author wants everyone to propose a move before checking.

reading.prompt: 2. Why should someone undo a move made to explain an idea?
options: The timer will not work after a first move.
The other player should start with the same positions.
The answer sheet needs to be removed.
There are only enough pieces for one card.
reading.explanation: Otherwise the instructions still refer to the previous board layout.

listening.prompt: 1. What does Rina need Ben to repeat?
options: The instructions for a thinking break
The details on the clue card
listening.explanation: She heard the letter D but missed the number five.

listening.prompt: 1. What is Rina doing during the thinking break?
options: Looking for the answer in the drawer
Checking what the blue card says
Considering what Ben could do next
listening.explanation: She postpones the blue hint to consider the reply first.

listening.prompt: 1. What does Ben do after showing a reply move?
options: Replaces the card with the next puzzle
Puts his piece back to its original square
Tells Rina to start over from the window
listening.explanation: He resets his piece to let Rina give another idea.

listening.prompt: 2. What does Ben want to do before playing a timed game?
options: Finish a game with the helper
Read the full answer to the third card
listening.explanation: He is interested in the timer but is unsure about committing to a full match.

listening.prompt: 2. When can Ben have a go at pressing it?
options: Immediately, during the current pair's game
During a brief demonstration at two
When the beginner board is full again
listening.explanation: The helper says the demo starts at two.

listening.prompt: 2. Why might Rina still be able to play if Ben changes tables?
options: The helper will cancel the timed game.
She is taking the dark pieces home.
She plans to wait for Ben to finish.
listening.explanation: The helper has another name waiting for a place.

grammar.explanation: Use stop + -ing to say an action ends. Use stop + to + verb when someone pauses one action in order to do another. Need, want and decide often take a to-infinitive. Finish and avoid take an -ing form.

examples.before: Please stop to move pieces during the break.
examples.after: Please stop moving pieces during the break.
examples.why: Players should end the action of moving pieces.

examples.before: He stopped checking the number before he placed the piece.
examples.after: He stopped to check the number before he placed the piece.
examples.why: The revised version shows that he paused in order to check.

examples.before: We finished to set up the board.
examples.after: We finished setting up the board.

questions.prompt: They wanted ___ the timer without starting a full match.
I avoid ___ an answer until both players have a go.
I need you ___ the letter and number slowly.
questions.explanation: Need plus an object can take a to-infinitive.

questions.prompt: Rina finished ___ the pieces before she read the clue.
Which explains that Rina paused because she wanted to think?
questions.explanation: Stop to think gives the purpose of the pause.

questions.prompt: Do you enjoy ___ without a timer?
The partners decided ___ a third card.
Which means Ben no longer touched the pieces?
options: Ben stopped to move the pieces.
Ben moved the pieces to stop.
questions.explanation: Stop plus moving means that he ended that action.

grammar.transfer: Write a paragraph about a new pair. Use stop to check once, stop moving with a different meaning, plus need to, finish -ing and avoid -ing. Read it aloud and ask where each participant pauses or resumes.

vocabulary.meaning: one small box on the board
vocabulary.example: The white piece starts on the middle square.

vocabulary.meaning: a device that measures the time available
vocabulary.example: The players have a different button on each side of the timer.

vocabulary.meaning: one of the objects moved in a board game
vocabulary.example: Put the dark piece on the next line.
We set up the board while Lucy read the card.

vocabulary.meaning: the arrangement or place of the pieces
vocabulary.example: Put the pieces back in the starting position.

vocabulary.meaning: offer an idea for someone to consider
vocabulary.example: Can you suggest a move for the other player?

vocabulary.meaning: stop an activity for a short time
vocabulary.example: I need to take a thinking break.

vocabulary.meaning: a piece of information that can help you find an answer
vocabulary.example: The card gives a clue about one square.
Have a go after your partner tries.

vocabulary.meaning: tell a group something out loud or publicly
vocabulary.example: They will announce the demo before the game begins.
I can concentrate with fewer pieces on the board.

vocabulary.meaning: limited by a set period on a clock
vocabulary.example: She would rather watch a timed match first.

speaking.audience: A new participant and their partner at Table Three
speaking.first: Give a two-minute introduction and then act out the first three exchanges. Explain reading and placing roles, make the thinking break rule clear, and point out the difference between the clue and the answer.
speaking.change: The new participant says a countdown makes them nervous. They would still like to see the clock used before they leave.
speaking.second: Make a second take for the same pair. Explain what they can watch, where they can continue, and how to change tables without leaving their partner alone.
checklist: Tell both people their first role
Model a polite request to pause
Explain when to use the answer sheet
Offer the demo without pushing a full match

writing.first: Write 125–155 words explaining how to welcome a waiting beginner, start a card and introduce the clock demo. Include what to do after a piece was moved to show an idea.
writing.change: The demo is delayed by twenty minutes while two players finish a match. Several people waiting by the window missed the announcement.
writing.second: Write a short update for the window board and a 60–80 word note to the new helper, with what to offer while people wait.
checklist: Choose the right information for each audience
Use clear time and sequence words
Explain one step after the delay

immersion.goal: Make a short onboarding kit that lets two newcomers practice without needing to know a full game's rules.
constraints: Both learners suggest moves before checking
Any demonstrated move must be reset
immersion.change: Only one blue clue card is available for the whole room, and three pairs want help at once.
deliverables: Draw a simple grid with labeled practice squares and two movable markers
Write one brief observation question and a clue that points at a square without giving a full answer
Build a four-step welcome sign and a waiting list with roles
Give a second spoken welcome showing how you share the single clue
checklist: The labels on the example grid can be said and understood
The clue hints rather than answers
Players know when to reset and switch jobs
The revised help plan can serve all three pairs
